sections.body_en:
The modern food industry makes use of many “food additives,” such as: emulsifiers, stabilizers, humectants, anti-caking agents, flavor enhancers and food colorings. Let us explain further: when one wishes to combine two substances that by nature do not combine, such as water and oil for the production of chocolate or dairy desserts, one uses an “emulsifier,” which binds and joins the two. Since sometimes, even after using an emulsifier, the two substances tend to separate, one uses a “stabilizer,” which keeps the substances joined. To preserve the moisture of products that tend to dry out, one uses “humectants.” When one wishes to prevent food from clumping, so that it remains attractive, soft and flexible, one uses “anti-caking” agents. When one wishes to turn a liquid product into a thick one, such as a dairy dessert made from liquid milk, one uses thickeners such as gelatin. When one wishes food products to keep for a long time, one uses preservatives and antioxidants. One also uses flavor enhancers, whose action is intended to accentuate certain flavors and to dissipate the sensation of other flavors.

Almost all of these basic industrial products are manufactured abroad, and therefore when their basis is from plants, they generally pose no halakhic questions. But when they are produced from animals, they are generally forbidden, because they are produced from impure animals, such as pigs and sheratzim (creeping creatures), or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha.1

When wine or wine vinegar of gentiles is mixed into food, there is the problem of stam yeinam (ordinary wine of gentiles), and if there is not sixty times its quantity, the food is forbidden (above 34:9; SA 134:2-3). When ingredients from dairy products are mixed into food, one must check whether they are forbidden as ḥalav nokhrim (milk of gentiles), and whether the product remains parve.

As halakha, since the consumer is not capable of knowing all the food additives and their halakhic status, responsible supervision is needed for all industrial food products, and without supervision one should not eat industrial food.

Having learned the halakhic rule for the consumer, let us explain the details of the laws of food additives.

notes_en.en: In many countries of the world, including Israel, food additives are labeled according to the European classification, represented by the letter E (Europe), which classifies the substances according to their function, with each hundred numbers having a particular function. Substances used as food colorings are labeled with the numbers 100 to 199, that is, E100-E199 (their law will be explained in halakha 5). The next hundred is devoted to preservatives, and their numbers are 200-299. Acidity regulators and antioxidants are numbered 300-399. Thickeners, emulsifiers and stabilizers are numbered 400-499. Gelatin is included in this hundred and its label is E441, and glycerin is E422. In the 500-599 series are anti-caking agents. In the 600-699 series are flavor enhancers. In the 700-799 series are antibiotic substances to prevent the growth of bacteria. In the 900-999 series are glazing agents, flavor intensifiers, sweeteners, foaming agents and more. These are the principal substances used in the food industry.

sections.title_en: The Halakhic Questions Regarding Food Additives
sections.body_en:
There are three main questions regarding the law of food additives. The first: what is the law when, in the course of the production process, the forbidden food becomes unfit to eat? Does the prohibition lapse from it, and is it considered panim ḥadashot (“a new entity”), or perhaps, since it is intended for the food industry, does its prohibition remain upon it?2

The second: when the forbidden ingredient is nullified in sixty, when does it have a significant effect on the food, so that consequently it is not nullified, according to the law of a ma'amid (an ingredient that gives the food its form) (above 34:6), and when is its effect faint, so that it is nullified?3

The third: even when the forbidden food additive does not have the law of a ma'amid, a Jew is forbidden to mix it into food le-khatḥila (above 34:13), and the question is what the law is when a gentile mixed it into food for gentiles and for Jews.4

notes_en.en: When a food has become unfit for human consumption, there is no longer a Torah prohibition in it, but according to most poskim it is forbidden to eat it by rabbinic law, and it is also forbidden to mix it intentionally into another food. So is the halakha (above 34:7, note 8). But if it has also become unfit for a dog to eat, some say that it has completely lost its status as food, and its prohibition has lapsed permanently, and it is permitted to mix it into permitted food (Aḥiezer 3:33; Ḥazon Naḥum 1:61; Yabi'a Omer vol. 8 YD 11), and some say that be-di'avad, if it has already been mixed in, it is permitted to eat the mixture (Har Tzvi YD 83). And some say that if it became unfit for a dog to eat as part of its preparation to become a food additive, its prohibition does not lapse, and it is like sourdough or yeast, which, although they have become unfit for a dog to eat, render forbidden the dough or wine made with them, since this is their purpose (based on Tosefta Beitza 1:5; Ḥelkat Yo'av YD 11; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:5). Similarly, the poskim disagreed regarding a food that became unfit for human consumption and in addition underwent a profound change of form, whether it is permitted to mix it into food le-khatḥila. The basis for this is the law of musk. The musk deer has a scent gland from which a pleasant fragrance is produced, which is also used to perfume foods. According to the Ramah and the Rosh (Berakhot 6:35), since the source of the fragrant substance is blood, the prohibition of blood applies to it, and it is forbidden to mix it into food. However, in practice the accepted ruling follows the opinion of Rabbeinu Yona (on the Rif, Berakhot 31b), that it is permitted to mix musk into foods, because the blood has changed completely: in its color, its taste and its smell, and it is like a new creation – “a new entity has come here.” The Ran added and explained that in addition to the musk having changed completely, it has also become unfit to eat, and therefore the prohibition has lapsed from it. This is also the consensus of most poskim: when a forbidden substance has changed completely and has become unfit for human consumption, its prohibition has lapsed and it is permitted to mix it into food. But if the change did not render it unfit for human consumption, even though it changed greatly, it remains forbidden and it is forbidden to mix it into food (Radbaz, the Gra, Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥazon Ish, Aḥiezer 2:11; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:5). Some are stringent and hold that the entire permission is on condition that the change took place naturally, but if the change was brought about by a deliberate human action, the food remains forbidden (Or Le-Tziyon 1, OḤ 34; Mishneh Halakhot 16:21). And some say that if a person's actions spoiled the food and also turned it into something new, even though the aim was to make it into a food additive, it is permitted. But if they merely broke down the forbidden food into separate substances, there is no new entity here and it remains forbidden (Tzitz Eliezer, introduction to vol. 4, in the name of Rav Yeḥezkel Abramsky; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:41).

As we have learned (above 30:7), the Sages forbade cheese of gentiles because they place in it the skin of the stomach of a nevela. From this the Responsa of the Rashba 3:214 learned that any forbidden substance that was put into permitted food in order to improve it is not nullified in it, even if there is sixty times its quantity. His words were cited as halakha in the Beit Yosef YD 134; Magen Avraham 442:1; Melamed Le-ho'il 2:41, and others. On the other hand, according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 3:13), cheese of gentiles is forbidden because the stomach skin gives the cheese its form, and a ma'amid is not nullified, and one cannot learn from this a prohibition for something that improves a food but does not give it its form. From his words the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Mahadura Tinyana YD 56) learned that one may permit beer into which nevela meat was put in order to dissipate its sharpness, since the meat does not give the beer its form, and the taste of the nevela is not discernible but merely improves the taste of the beer. And since even according to the Rashba the prohibition is rabbinic, in a dispute regarding a rabbinic law the halakha follows the lenient opinion. So wrote the Seridei Esh 2:21 regarding glycerin from nevelot; and the Or Le-Tziyon vol. 1 OḤ 34 regarding citric acid. Some of the lenient authorities explain that even the Rashba was stringent only when the forbidden substance improves the food noticeably, but when its taste is not discernible and the improvement it causes the food is slight, it is nullified in sixty (Maḥatzit Ha-shekel 447:45; Maharsham 3:234; Minḥat Yitzḥak 9:168).
According to the Minḥat Yitzḥak 6:71, preservatives made from forbidden substances, such as glycerin from nevelot, do not have the law of a ma'amid, since they merely preserve what was created without them. According to Rav Eliyahu, since without it the food would spoil, it is considered a ma'amid (Ha-kashrut Ka-halakha vol. 1, 24:25).

According to the Radbaz (3:547), the entire permission according to the Rambam that was cited in the previous note applies when the forbidden substance was mixed into the food unintentionally, but if a gentile intentionally mixed a forbidden substance into the food, even if there was sixty times its quantity and the improvement from the forbidden substance is slight, even according to the Rambam and those who agree with him it is forbidden to buy it from the gentile, since the prohibition of nullifying a forbidden substance le-khatḥila also includes a prohibition of buying it from someone who nullified it intentionally. So wrote the Shiyurei Berakha 99:5, and the Beit Yehuda wrote similarly (p. 115b). On the other hand, most Aḥaronim disagreed with the Radbaz and wrote that since the gentile is not commanded regarding this, he is permitted to nullify forbidden substances in sixty, and after they have been nullified a Jew is permitted to buy these foods from him. So wrote the Maharam of Lublin 104; Noda Bi-Yehuda Mahadura Tinyana YD 56; Yad Ha-melekh, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:25; Darkei Teshuva 108:20; Beit Yitzḥak 142:8; Yabi'a Omer 7, YD 7, and others.
However, the opinion of those who permit is on condition that the gentile prepared the foods for gentiles, but if he regularly sells his products to Jews as well, it turns out that he nullifies the forbidden substance for them, and consequently they are forbidden to Jews (as explained above 34:13). So wrote Rabbi Akiva Eiger 99:5, in the name of the Rivash 498. And when the buyers do not know whether the gentile mixed a forbidden substance into a food that he regularly sells to Jews as well, for example, it is a food into which sometimes a kosher plant-based additive is mixed and sometimes a forbidden animal-based additive, and there is sixty times its quantity, some say that according to the opinion of those who permit (who disagree with the Radbaz and those who agree with him), it is permitted to buy from him (Minḥat Yitzḥak vol. 2 28:20, based on Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 7:59; Taz 99:10; Pri To'ar 99:9). And according to the Pri Ḥadash 13, Rabbi Akiva Eiger and the Ḥazon Ish 37:13, even if the buyers did not know about the nullification, the food is forbidden to them, since the forbidden substance was nullified in it for them.

sections.body_en:
Gelatin (E441) is produced from the protein collagen, which is found in bones and hides. Its function is to stabilize and set sweets, ice creams, dairy desserts and the like. The large factories produce it from impure animals, or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha. In the production process, the bones and hides are soaked in lime in order to draw out of them the unneeded liquids and substances; what remains is ground into powder, mixed with water and heated, until the collagen molecules change their composition and become gelatin.

Some permit it, since in the process of making gelatin the bones and hides change their nature and lose all their taste until they are no longer fit even for a dog to eat, and “a new entity has come here,” in which there is no prohibition. And if it is produced from the hard part of the bones, there is an additional reason to permit it, for some say that this part was never considered food, and the prohibition never applied to it from the outset (Aḥiezer 3:33; Har Tzvi YD 83; Yabi'a Omer vol. 8 YD 11). And some forbid it, because the creation of gelatin is not considered the creation of something new, but merely the separation of the collagen from the other substances, and consequently the Torah prohibition that applied to the bones and hides of impure animals and nevelot remains on the gelatin that was separated from them. And it is not nullified in sixty, since it has the law of a ma'amid, which is not nullified in sixty (Igrot Moshe YD 2:23, 27; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:5).

In practice, those who wish to be lenient may do so, since the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, for in practice gelatin has no taste; rather, it sets and stabilizes, and the rule that a ma'amid is not nullified even in a thousand is rabbinic (above 34:6). In addition, it is possible that some of those who were stringent in the past would also agree that nowadays the collagen undergoes a chemical process that makes the gelatin be considered “a new entity.” On the other hand, however, since nowadays it is easy to obtain gelatin produced from pure animals that were slaughtered properly, or from the skins of pure fish, le-khatḥila it is proper not to use gelatin produced from a forbidden source.

Glycerin (glycerol – E422) is one of the components of fat in the living body, and its purpose is to store energy for times of hunger and to create an insulating layer for the body. In the food industry it is used for moisturizing, thickening, sweetening, preserving and more, and sometimes it suffices to use a minute quantity of it. In the large factories around the world it is produced from impure animals such as pigs, or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha. Today there are plant-based and synthetic substitutes for glycerin produced from animals.

Some say that since in the course of producing glycerin from animals there was a stage at which it became unfit for a dog to eat and became putrid, its prohibition lapsed, and even though it became fit to eat again, “a new entity” has come here and there is no prohibition in it. In addition, often it does not amount to a proportion of one sixtieth, and consequently it is nullified. And one cannot claim that it is a ma'amid, because generally its effect on the food product is not as discernible as that of an ordinary ma'amid, and often it performs its action together with products that are kosher, in which case this is a matter of zeh ve-zeh gorem (“this and that cause it”) (above 34:6), in which there is no longer a prohibition.

On the other hand, some say that glycerin is not considered “a new entity,” since it was merely separated from the fatty acids to which it was attached. And the fact that it became putrid is not considered as having made it unfit to eat, because it became so within a deliberate process whose aim is to prepare it for eating. Therefore, when it is the only ma'amid, the entire food must be forbidden. And even when it is not the only ma'amid, it is forbidden to mix it in intentionally, and if it was mixed in, le-khatḥila one should not eat the food in which it is mixed. And so the customary ruling is. Therefore, one must make sure that the glycerin is produced from pure animals that were slaughtered according to halakha, or from vegetable oil, or from a synthetic source.5

notes_en.en: Glycerin is produced by separating fatty compounds of the “triglyceride” type into a glycerin molecule and three molecules of fatty acids. Initially, about a hundred and fifty years ago, glycerin was used to thicken and sweeten alcoholic spirits. It was produced by boiling, which did not render it unfit to eat, and consequently it was agreed that using it is forbidden (Darkei Teshuva 103:70; Yismaḥ Levav YD 24). With the development of the food industry, glycerin also began to be used as a stabilizer, emulsifier, preservative, anti-crystallization agent, and for other uses that are not for flavor. Nowadays, during the refining of glycerin, substances that render it unfit for a dog to eat, such as caustic soda, are mixed into it. Some say that at this stage its prohibition lapses (Ma'aseh Ḥoshev 5:12, 13). According to most poskim, since its taste was spoiled because of another substance mixed into it, and after that substance is removed from it the glycerin becomes fit to eat again, the prohibition of the glycerin remains in place (Ḥavot Da'at 103:1; Ḥelkat Yo'av YD 11; Or Le-Tziyon 1:34). The Aḥaronim further disagreed as to whether separating the glycerin from the fatty acids is considered “a new entity”: on the one hand, one could say that since the triglyceride compound breaks down into different molecules, this is a new entity. On the other hand, one could say that a change that makes a substance a new entity is a change in the internal arrangement of the molecule, and since the internal arrangement of the glycerin molecule did not change, its law remains as it was. In practice, the Seridei Esh 2:21 was lenient, and so too explained the Tzitz Eliezer 6:16. On the other hand, the Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:5 was stringent, and most poskim lean toward this in practice.

sections.body_en:
Food colorings are intended to give food a fresh and attractive appearance, and sometimes also to cover up defects. Originally, food manufacturers used natural substances produced from fruits, vegetables and insects. With the development of modern industry, colorings were developed from synthetic materials such as petroleum and coal, which are cheap and whose color is stronger and more durable, and they are all kosher, since synthetic materials pose no kashrut questions. In recent years it has become clear that they may be harmful to health, especially to children during their period of development. Following this, a process is taking place in which more manufacturers are returning to the use of natural food colorings.

Most natural food colorings are produced from plants abroad, and therefore they pose no kashrut problem, except for E163, whose color is between red and blue, and which is sometimes produced from the remnants of grapes that were pressed for wine, in which case it involves the prohibition of stam yeinam (above 29:2).

Food colorings produced from animals are forbidden. The most common of them are carminic acid (E120), which yields a red color and is produced from scale insects, and the food coloring E161g, which is sometimes produced from shrimp-crustaceans and other impure creatures.6

notes_en.en:
According to the Minḥat Ya'akov 74:5, a food into which a forbidden substance was mixed in order to give it color, and whose taste is not discernible, is permitted. From the Shakh YD 102:5 it is implied that it is forbidden. So wrote the Gra, and therefore the Mishna Berura 513:9 and most Aḥaronim leaned toward this. However, some say that if the food coloring produced from impure animals or nevelot reached a stage at which it was not fit to eat, for example, it underwent drying until it lost its taste, there is no longer a prohibition in it. As the Tiferet Tzvi YD 73 permitted wine whose red color was intensified by means of a powder made from flies that were dried and ground, and as the Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Shibbolei Ha-leket regarding the law of stomach skin. So too it is implied from the Shakh 114:21 that any food that has dried out like wood has lost its prohibition, as cited in the Pitḥei Teshuva 87:20.
On the other hand, according to the Pri Megadim, only stomach skin that has dried out loses its prohibition, since it does not return to its former state through cooking, but meat that was dried remains forbidden, since cooking restores it to its former state. According to the Noda Bi-Yehuda, Mahadura Kamma YD 26, only with regard to meat and milk, if the meat dried out like wood, it has lost its status as meat and there is no prohibition against cooking it with milk, but with regard to other prohibitions, drying out like wood does not cancel the prohibition. Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu added that even according to most of those who permit something that has dried out like wood, that is specifically when it is eaten not in its usual manner of eating, but if it is intended as a food coloring, it is eaten in its usual manner of eating and renders forbidden the foods colored with it. And even if there is sixty times the food coloring, it is not nullified, since its effect on the mixture is discernible, and its law is like that of a ma'amid, which is not nullified (Amma Davar 1:17). And so the accepted ruling is, that kashrut certification should not be given to products containing food colorings of animal origin that have undergone drying and have no taste, as I wrote above. However, be-di'avad, if they were put into a food, in a pressing situation one may rely on the opinion of the lenient authorities.
Among the food colorings known to be especially liable to harm health are: E102, E110, E124.

sections.body_en:
In many places in the world it is customary to coat fruits and sweets with shellac so that they look shiny and attractive. Shellac is a tree resin which, through the secretion of an insect called the lac bug, found in the region of Thailand and India, becomes solid and sticky, and in order to coat fruits and sweets with it, it is diluted with alcohol (its label is E904, from the series of glazing agents).

Some forbid fruits and sweets coated with shellac, since the substance secreted by the insect is what gives the shellac its form and causes it to stick to the fruits and sweets, and this substance is forbidden because it comes from an impure insect (Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu; Emek Ha-teshuva 66 in the name of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, and others).

And some permit them, because the substance that comes from the insect is hard as wood and its taste is bitter, and consequently it is nullified in the shellac according to the law of noten ta'am li-fgam (imparting a detrimental taste), which does not render its mixture forbidden. And the fact that it gives the coating its form is not considered being a ma'amid with regard to prohibitions of eating (see Igrot Moshe vol. 2 YD 24; Tola'at Shani 1, 6:42).

In practice, the custom is not to give kashrut certification to foods coated with shellac, and there is also no great need for it, since foods can be coated with a coating made of permitted substances. One who buys fruit that may have been coated with shellac should rinse it well, in order to remove its coating. And there is no need to worry that he may not succeed in removing all of it, since this is a sfek sfeika (double doubt) concerning a rabbinic law: the first doubt – perhaps the fruit was not coated with shellac, and if it was coated, perhaps it came off in the rinsing; the second doubt – even if shellac remained, perhaps the halakha follows those who permit it. And the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, since it does not impart taste to the food.

sections.title_en: Products Grown on a Forbidden Medium
sections.body_en:
A food that has become unfit for a dog to eat has lost its prohibition. However, when its unfitness for a dog serves people for the purpose of improving other foods, like sourdough put into dough (Tosefta Beitza 1:5), or yeast that ferments wine and beer, or sour milk that hastens the curdling of milk into cheese, it retains its significance and its prohibition, and renders forbidden the food that it improved.

Recently, in industrial food production, sour milk is no longer used to turn milk into soft cheese, nor is rennet used to curdle hard cheese, nor sourdough to leaven dough. Instead, special bacteria or yeast fungi (microorganisms) are taken and grown in a growth medium containing the substances on which they feed. As a result, they multiply and replicate rapidly, until after a few days millions of yeast fungi or bacteria are obtained, from which enzymes can also be produced. After they reach the required quantity, they are isolated from the growth medium and frozen in order to market them to factories. By means of the enzymes, hard cheeses are curdled; by means of the yeast fungi, dough is leavened and wine and beer are fermented; and by means of the bacteria, soft cheeses are prepared.

As halakha, even when the medium in which these tiny creatures are grown contains forbidden substances, the creatures that grow in it are considered kosher. First, because the growth medium is always composed also of kosher substances, without which the tiny creatures growing on it could not exist, and therefore they are considered to develop through zeh ve-zeh gorem, which is permitted be-di'avad (above 34:6). Furthermore, the tiny creatures that feed on the growth medium are not formed from it, but develop by virtue of the food it supplies them, and this is like an animal that eats forbidden foods, whose meat, according to most poskim, is permitted to eat. And even the stringent authorities agree that if it also feeds on other things, it is permitted.

However, there is a reason to distinguish and say that the forbidden food undergoes a complete process of digestion in the animal's body, and therefore its prohibition is nullified before it builds the cells of the animal's body, whereas these tiny creatures feed directly on the forbidden substance. Likewise, the reasoning of zeh ve-zeh gorem permits only be-di'avad, and nowadays kosher substitutes can be found for the forbidden substances that make up the growth medium. Therefore, the kashrut organizations require that the growth medium be composed of kosher substances. Only when this is not possible or is difficult to carry out do they rely on the lenient reasoning.7

notes_en.en:
Temura 31a: an animal that was fed vetch of idolatry together with kosher foods is fit for a sacrifice, and if it was fed only vetch of idolatry, it is forbidden for a sacrifice. Tosafot added (s.v. “she-yinka”) that it is also forbidden to eat. According to the Pleti (YD 60:1), this prohibition applies only if it ate foods that were forbidden because of the prohibition of idolatry, but if it ate other forbidden foods, it is permitted, since they have already been digested in the animal's intestines and have passed out of existence. According to the Shakh 60:5 and the Pri Ḥadash 5, whenever it ate foods from which benefit is forbidden, it is forbidden, since through the animal's eating one derives benefit from them indirectly, but if it ate foods that are forbidden only to eat, it is permitted. And according to the Rema (60:1), even if it ate foods that are forbidden to eat, but it ate only them all its life, it is forbidden.
Regarding bacteria and fungi: on the one hand, the medium on which they grow is always composed also of permitted substances without which they cannot exist, and so seemingly even according to the Rema they are permitted to eat. On the other hand, one could say that with an animal that ate forbidden foods we are lenient because by the time the forbidden food turns into a substance that nourishes its body's cells, it undergoes a long process of digestion and breakdown in the animal's intestines. However, the bacteria and fungi feed directly on the proteins and carbon produced from the forbidden food, and therefore perhaps there is a prohibition in them.
As halakha, since in any case they also feed on permitted food, be-di'avad they do not render the food forbidden, according to the law of zeh ve-zeh gorem (see Shevet Ha-levi 8:114; Devar Ḥevron OḤ 472; Amma Davar 1:60). But since it is possible to ensure that the medium is kosher, le-khatḥila one should not certify as kosher bacteria grown on a forbidden medium, except in cases where it is difficult to obtain a kosher medium.
[When yogurt was set using milk of gentiles and allowed to sour a great deal so that good bacteria would develop in it, by means of which more milk could be turned into fine yogurt, this starter culture is forbidden to a Jew, since it was created from milk of gentiles. Be-di'avad, when necessary, it will be possible to make kosher yogurt from the third generation: that is, to take this starter and make from it another yogurt, which is the first; from it to take a starter and make a second-generation yogurt; from it to make a starter and prepare a third-generation yogurt; and from that one it is permitted to take a starter to make yogurt of a Jew (Beit Yosef, end of 115). According to the Maharit Tzahalon (Yeshanot 81), it is permitted to use even the first starter, for since it set, this indicates that it contains no impure milk, and there is also no need to be concerned about traces of milk, since they are nullified in sixty. This is not nullifying a prohibition le-khatḥila: first, because it is doubtful whether there is impure milk there; second, he does not want the remnants of the impure milk, and consequently he does not wish to nullify it. And it is not considered a ma'amid, because the main setting is done by pure milk. So wrote the Responsa Ḥikrei Lev YD 139. See Kaf Ha-ḥayim 115:51, and Ḥalav Yisrael Ke-hilkhato 11:7.]

sections.body_en:
Medicines that do not have a pleasant taste do not require a hekhsher (kashrut certification). True, by rabbinic law a person is forbidden to eat a spoiled forbidden food, because by deciding to eat it he regards it as food that has not been spoiled, and consequently it is forbidden for him to eat it. However, when the purpose of swallowing is medical, the medicine is not regarded as food, and there is no prohibition in it.

However, tasty medicines, such as lozenges and syrups, as well as tasty vitamins that healthy people take to strengthen their health, le-khatḥila require a hekhsher. This responsibility rests on the health organizations, which must appoint an expert to check that the medicines and health supplements they give to the sick and the healthy are produced from kosher substances. The consumer too should prefer medicines and vitamins that have a hekhsher. But if he did not find them with a hekhsher, he may take tasty medicines and vitamins without a hekhsher. This is because in practice, the main substance in medicines and vitamins is not composed of non-kosher substances, and only regarding the substances that accompany the medicine is there a doubt as to whether they were produced from substances forbidden to eat. And since this is a very remote concern that it is almost impossible for the consumer to investigate, one should follow the majority and deem the medicine kosher. But vitamins and food supplements that are also eaten for enjoyment, and over which one must therefore also recite a birkat ha-nehenin (blessing over enjoyment) before eating them, may not be eaten without a hekhsher.

Toothpicks and lipsticks that have a flavor are permitted, because the concern that a non-kosher substance was mixed into them is very remote and very difficult to investigate, and therefore there is no need to be concerned about it. In addition, those who use toothpicks and lipsticks do not intend to eat the flavor in them. Those who wish to be scrupulous should prefer toothpicks and lipsticks without flavor or with kashrut certification.8

notes_en.en:
In the modern pharmaceutical industry, every medicine is composed of two types of substances: “active ingredients,” which perform the medical action, and “inactive ingredients,” which help form the medicine, regulate its dissolution on contact with liquids, coat it to prevent damage from water and air, and give it color so that it looks attractive and is easy to identify. In tasty medicines, the accompanying substance gives them flavor in order to make them easier to swallow or suck. As a rule, the active ingredients pose no kashrut problems, since they are produced from synthetic substances, and their taste is also very unpleasant. But there is a question regarding the kashrut of the auxiliary substances, which are sometimes produced from gelatin, glycerin or other substances concerning whose kashrut there is a halakhic doubt (as explained in halakhot 2-7). Likewise, there are substances produced from starch of the five species of grain, regarding which there is a doubt whether they are kosher for Pesaḥ (see Peninei Halakha, Pesaḥ 8, note 9).
There are two foundations for permitting non-tasty medicines produced from forbidden foods, and on the basis of each of them one can permit non-tasty medicines: a) when they became unfit to eat, their prohibition lapsed and they are permitted to everyone; b) according to most poskim, for the purpose of healing a sick person it is permitted to eat them not in the manner of enjoyment:
a) There is no Torah prohibition in a forbidden food that has become unfit for human consumption, such as a putrid nevela. However, according to most poskim, one who wishes to eat it thereby regards it as fit food, and it is forbidden for him to eat it by rabbinic law (Rambam and Rosh, above 34, note 8). But when the purpose of eating is healing, there is no prohibition in it according to the overwhelming majority of poskim (Ktav Sofer OḤ 111, Yad Yehuda 103, long commentary 8, Igrot Moshe OḤ 2:92, Tzitz Eliezer 6:16, and many others). True, according to the Sha'agat Aryeh 75, even when the purpose is medical, a person regards it as food and it is forbidden. However, it is possible that even he would agree that in a mixture with permitted substances that make up the main part of the medicine, as is customary with medicines, there is no prohibition.
b) According to the Ritva in the name of the Ra'ah, a sick person who is not in danger is forbidden to eat a forbidden food even not in the manner of enjoyment. On the other hand, some say that according to the basic law even a healthy person is permitted to swallow a forbidden food not in the manner of enjoyment, but le-khatḥila one should not do so (Ra'avya, Mordekhai, Agudda, Issur Ve-hetter He-arokh 32:19-20, Shakh 155:13-14). The halakha follows the opinion of the Rambam (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:8) and Orḥot Ḥayim, that a sick person who is not in danger is permitted to eat a forbidden food for the sake of his healing, and a healthy person is forbidden. So wrote the Tzitz Eliezer 6:16; Minḥat Shlomo 1:17; Shevet Ha-levi 7:135, and others.
When the medicines are tasty, a question arises lest the flavoring substances were made from forbidden substances. Nevertheless, since it is almost impossible for the consumer to investigate this (often it is a trade secret), and in practice in the vast majority of medicines and vitamins the flavoring substances are from kosher substances, as halakha one should follow the majority (SA 110:3; and see Be-tzel Ha-ḥokhma 4:174). And although this foundation suffices for the halakha, one can add further considerations for leniency: a) Often it is a matter of a rabbinic doubt, for example when the flavoring substance is lactose produced from milk of gentiles, whose prohibition is rabbinic and also disputed, or tartaric acid produced from wine that was perhaps forbidden as stam yeinam, and regarding which there is also a dispute, for perhaps since it has changed completely it is considered something new and its prohibition has lapsed. Or it undergoes chemical processes regarding which the poskim disagreed whether they cause the prohibition to lapse, as we learned (in halakhot 3-4) regarding gelatin and glycerin (true, a concern was raised that the flavoring substance may be produced from a Torah prohibition, such as Civet Absolute, made from the secretion of the civet, or Castoreum, made from the secretion of the beaver; but the main consideration for leniency returns, that one follows the majority, all the more so when this is a very remote concern, since these are rare substances that are hardly used in industrial drug production). b) The quantity of the problematic substance is much smaller than a kezayit, and some say that ḥatzi shi'ur (less than the minimum measure) was permitted for a sick person (Ha-ḥinukh 313, Darkei Teshuva 155:18, Tzitz Eliezer 6:16. And see Har Tzvi YD 97, who added a further consideration, that perhaps the forbidden substance is considered eaten not in its usual manner of eating, since it was mixed with the active medicinal substance, which is bitter). However, le-khatḥila, the manufacturers of medicines and those who market them, who have the ability to investigate the matter thoroughly, must ensure that all tasty medicines and vitamins are made from kosher ingredients only. Likewise the consumer, when he has two options before him, should prefer the kosher medicine (Rema 155:3).
Regarding lipstick and toothpicks, so ruled many rabbis, and so wrote Rav Lior in Devar Ḥevron YD 2:95; and Mo'adim p. 91, regarding Pesaḥ. And some were stringent (Ha-kashrut 21:51).

sections.body_en:
Alcohol can be produced from foods that contain sugar by turning the foods into liquids (such as grape juice) and fermenting them with yeast (yeast fungi), which turns the sugar in them into alcohol (ethanol). By heating the liquids and evaporating the alcohol, one can distill the alcohol and isolate it from the liquids with which it was mixed.

In practice, although the taste and smell of alcohol are completely different from the liquids from which it was distilled, it is agreed as halakha that the law of alcohol is like the law of the food from which it was produced. Therefore, alcohol that was distilled from wine of gentiles and made into a drink such as brandy is forbidden to drink (Responsa Rivash 255). And alcohol produced from grains of ḥametz, such as whisky and beer, is considered ḥametz by Torah law.9

Spirits and whisky: Just as all foods and drinks require a hekhsher, so do spirits of all kinds. However, regarding whisky, since the way it is made from grains is known, many poskim permitted drinking it without a hekhsher, and so many are accustomed. And although there are producers who customarily age the whisky in wooden casks that previously absorbed the taste of wine of gentiles, and the taste may be absorbed into the whisky, since the wine that comes out of the casks does not amount to a quantity that imparts taste, they ruled that the whisky is permitted. However, their permission was said regarding genuine, quality whisky whose rules of production are known, and violating them is considered harming the consumer; but in the case of cheap whisky, or whisky into which additional flavors were mixed, or other spirits, one should not drink them without a hekhsher, lest forbidden foods were mixed into them.

Similarly, in various places in the world where it is known that the beer or other spirits are made from kosher substances, and where people are careful to preserve the tradition of the way they are produced and not to mix any other substance into them, the local rabbis permit drinking them without a hekhsher. But when there is no clear knowledge about this, one must return to the basic rule, not to eat any food or drink that has no hekhsher.10

notes_en.en: Some say that only alcohol from wine of gentiles, from which benefit is forbidden, is forbidden like the wine, but alcohol produced from another forbidden food is not forbidden by Torah law, and if it was produced from a rabbinically forbidden food, it is permitted. Therefore, if by mistake whisky was not sold before Pesaḥ, be-di'avad it is permitted to drink it after Pesaḥ. Likewise, alcohol produced from milk of gentiles is kosher to eat (Penei Yehoshua OḤ end of 13, Beit Efrayim OḤ 48). However, according to most poskim, and so it was ruled as halakha, the law of alcohol is like the law of the drink from which it was produced, and therefore whisky is considered ḥametz by Torah law, and consequently it is forbidden after Pesaḥ by rabbinic law. And alcohol produced from milk of gentiles is forbidden like milk of gentiles (Mas'at Binyamin 58, Sha'ar Efrayim 4, Mishna Berura 442:4; Minḥat Yitzḥak 7:59).

Some forbid whisky without a hekhsher, because it was aged in casks in which wine of gentiles had previously been aged, intentionally, so that it would absorb some of its taste (Rav Moshe Yehuda Landau). However, many permitted it for various reasons: according to the Taz, the taste of the wine is nullified if it is less than one sixth, and even according to those who are stringent that its taste is nullified in sixty, it seems that in practice its taste is not discernible. They also raised further reasons: that the wine absorbed in the wooden casks merely dissipates taste and is not meant to impart a good taste. And furthermore, that there is doubt whether it was aged at all in a cask that previously held wine (Igrot Moshe YD 1:62; Minḥat Yitzḥak 2:28; Mishneh Halakhot 10:108; Minḥat Asher 1:44). However, it seems that all this applies to quality whisky whose methods of production are known and which producers are careful not to change, but other whisky may have had forbidden substances mixed into it, and one should not permit it without a hekhsher; and the same law applies to other spirits.

sections.body_en:
A Jew is forbidden to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by Torah law, such as nevelot and tereifot, as well as the meat of impure domestic and wild animals, as well as impure fish or sheratzim. But it is permitted to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by rabbinic law, such as milk of gentiles and bishulei goyim (food cooked by gentiles). An exception to the rule is the prohibition of ḥelev of a pure animal: although it is forbidden to eat by Torah law, it is permitted to trade in it, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:24): “And the fat of that which dies of itself, and the fat of that which is torn by beasts, may be used for any other service; but you shall in no way eat of it.” Thus the prohibition is only to eat it, but it is permitted to do work with it, and consequently also to trade in it (Pesaḥim 23a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:16-18; SA 117:1).

Just as it is forbidden to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by Torah law, so it is forbidden to raise impure animals for gentiles to eat (Baḥ, Shakh 117:14). Likewise, it is forbidden to take them as a pledge for a loan (Rema ibid.).

However, if one slaughtered a pure animal in order to eat it and it turned out to be a nevela or tereifa, it is permitted to sell it, as it is stated (Devarim 14:21): “You shall not eat of anything that dies of itself; you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner.” Likewise, if impure animals came into a person's possession by chance, for example, he spread his net and impure animals were caught in it, he is permitted to sell them to a gentile promptly (Mishna Shevi'it 7:3-4). And he is forbidden to delay their sale so that their price will rise (Rema 117:1).

Likewise, if a gentile owed money to a Jew and repaid his debt in forbidden foods, if there is a concern that if he does not accept them he will lose his debt, he is permitted to accept them in order to save his money, and he should hasten to sell them to a gentile (SA and Rema 117:1).11

It is permitted to trade in impure animals that are not intended for eating, such as horses for riding, donkeys for travel, a dog for guarding or as a pet, and impure fish for ornament (Shakh 117:1).

notes_en.en:
According to most Rishonim, the prohibition of trading is by Torah law (Tosafot, Rosh, Ra'ah, Ran, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Agudda, Tashbetz, Or Zarua and others). According to the Ra'avad, Rashba, Terumat Ha-deshen and Mabit, the prohibition is rabbinic.
Some forbid buying forbidden foods in order to feed them to one's gentile workers (Rema 117:1), and some permit it, since he is not trading in them or dealing with them, but merely giving them to the workers to eat (Shakh 3, Pri Ḥadash), and many are accustomed to be lenient about this (Maharam Schick 136, Ḥokhmat Adam, Ḥelkat Binyamin [?] 10).
When a Jew is permitted to trade in forbidden foods that came into his possession by chance in order to prevent a loss, as explained above, some say that he is permitted to sell them to a fellow Jew so that the latter may sell them (Taz, Rabbi Akiva Eiger). And some forbid it (Baḥ, Shakh). It seems that when the Jew into whose possession the forbidden foods came does not know how to trade in them, he is permitted to sell them through his fellow (Meshivat Nefesh YD 39, as cited in Darkei Teshuva 117:15).

sections.body_en:
In recent years scientists have succeeded in developing meat artificially by replicating stem cells (cells that have not completed their differentiation) taken from the meat of animals. If this development succeeds commercially, a revolution may take place in the meat market: people will stop raising and slaughtering billions of cows and chickens, the price of meat will fall, and the pollution involved in raising animals will cease.

Some say that the law of such meat will be identical to the law of the stem cell from which it developed, since everything derives from it. Thus, if it is taken from pork, its law will be like pork. And if it is taken from the meat of a domestic animal or a bird that was slaughtered properly, its law will be like kosher meat, which is permitted to eat but forbidden to mix with milk. And some say that since the initial cell is tiny and insignificant, it is nullified among the billions of cells that developed from it, and they are considered entirely “a new entity,” and therefore even if the first cell was from a pig, it is kosher, and even if it was from a calf, its law is like that of parve food. It seems that the first opinion is correct, that the essence of the food is determined by the first cell that generated it.12

notes_en.en: Among the lenient authorities: Rav Reisman, Teḥumin 34; Rav Dov Lior, Rav Ze'ev Weitman, Teḥumin 36. Among the stringent authorities: Rav Yehuda Spitz, Teḥumin 35; Rav Ya'akov Ariel, Teḥumin 36; Rav Dr. Ḥanokh Kahan, Ha-ma'ayan, Tevet 5776. It is possible that even according to the reasoning of the lenient authorities, as long as natural meat from animals is common and the artificial meat resembles it, there is room to forbid it with milk because of mar'it ayin (appearance of wrongdoing) (see SA 66:9-10; 87:4).
